new_statements.quote: El tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo (Kager, 2007), y por lo mismo no presenta un acento léxicamente contrastivo como el español. El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado. [...] El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas, que se pueden caracterizar aproximativamente como los constituyentes prosódicos que agrupan un núcleo léxico y todos sus satélites, incluyendo determinantes, clíticos, preposiciones, etcétera [...] [fn. 2, p. 87:] La prominencia relativa del acento léxico inicial no es la misma en todas las variantes del tseltal. Es más importante, por ejemplo, en la variante de Bachajón que en la de Oxchuc.
new_statements.translation: Tseltal is a fixed-accent language (Kager 2007), and therefore does not have a lexically contrastive accent as Spanish does. The accent falls on the last syllable of phonological phrases, and in particular at the end of the utterance. [...] The final accent does not properly concern words, but phonological phrases, which can be characterized approximately as the prosodic constituents grouping a lexical head and all its satellites, including determiners, clitics, prepositions, etc. [...] [fn. 2, p. 87:] The relative prominence of the initial lexical accent is not the same in all varieties of Tseltal. It is more important, for example, in the Bachajón variety than in that of Oxchuc.
new_statements.citation: Polian, Gilles. 2013. Gramática del tseltal de Oxchuc, Tomo I. México: Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropología Social (Publicaciones de la Casa Chata).
new_statements.locator: §3.2 'Acento y prosodia', pp. 85-86 (main text) and p. 87 fn. 2 (Bachajón); exceptions p. 85-86 fn. 1 and §3.8.10 'Transfonologización del acento tónico', p. 123. In the saved txt: lines 3364-3466 and 5123-5136.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: publisher URL https://materiales.aldelim.org/materiales/Gramatica_1.pdf still returns HTTP 200, 5117541 bytes, so the open-source status stands). Locator check: the text layer = printed pp. 85-87 (PDF pages 82-84; running headers '3.2. Acento y prosodia' and the InDesign slug 'GRAMA_TOMO I_18JUNIO.indb 85/86/87'), the text layer = printed p. 123 §3.8.10 (PDF page 120). All three quoted pieces are there verbatim: (a) p. 85 'El tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo (Kager, 2007), y por lo mismo no presenta un acento léxicamente contrastivo como el español. El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado.' (b) p. 86 'El acento final no co…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive, predictable accent on the last syllable of the phonological phrase (a lexical word plus its enclitics and satellites), hence on the final syllable of a word pronounced in isolation or phrase-finally (At'éj, At'ej-ón, At'ej-on=íx); realized by an F0 rise and vowel lengthening, not by intensity; non-final phrases may be unaccented. Separately, lexical roots may carry an emphatic prominence (lengthening only) on their initial syllable, which drives second-syllable syncope; Polian states this root-initial prominence is more important in Bachajón than in Oxchuc. Position = final; domain explicitly phrasal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; a root-initial emphatic lengthening ('acento de énfasis en su sílaba inicial'), especially on the main predicate and focused words, stronger in Bachajón (fn. 2). How it interacts with the final phrasal accent 'todavía requiere más investigación'. (Gerdel 1974, Oxchuc: secondary stress on the first or second syllable of the stress group; Kaufman 1971 per SPA 1979 and Shklovsky 2005: root/word-initial stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Old Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans with lexical initial accent: (')áko 'bee sp.', páta 'guava', tsíma 'gourd' (fn. 1). Spanish loans (§3.8.10 p. 123): consonant-final loans become oxytone (axúx, wakáx); vowel-final loans usually keep Spanish penult stress (káxa, xíla) alternating with oxytone kaxá, xilá, the latter typical of older monolinguals. Smith 1999 gives the same loan pattern (lóbleh 'oak').
new_statements.domain_note: The source says in so many words that the final accent belongs to the phonological phrase, not the word ('no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas'); clitics following a word take the accent. Coded here as fixed: final syllable with domain = phrase (alternative code: phrase-level prominence only). The data are Oxchuc-based; the general statement is framed for 'el tseltal', and only fn. 2 addresses Bachajón directly (stronger root-initial prominence).
new_statements.identity_note: tzel1255 is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING code (family book1242): ISO 639-3 tzb 'Bachajón Tzeltal' was retired by change request 2008-060 ('Merge with Tzeltal [tzh]', effective 2009-01-16; the one Glottolog reference for this key is that change request). Bachajón is the northern dialect of Tseltal, language-level unit tzel1254 [tzh], which is already a catalog unit (fixed-dominant final, evidence carried from Wikipedia/Smith 1999). Under the census/code-currency law a retired code does not make a separate language, so this key should not become a separate unit; the earlier catalog read ( A/B, 2026-09-12) already judged it duplicate entry of tzel1254. The statement quoted here (Polian 2013, first-hand, held by the project) is the one the tzel1254 search recommends should replace the Wikipedia/Smith citation for tzel1254, with domain coded phrase and a note that root-initial prominence is stronger in Bachajón (Polian 2013 p. 87 fn. 2). The only Bachajón-specific descriptions are Slocum et al. 1999 (grammar sketch, read, silent on accent) and Robles Uribe 1962 (print only, not read). Nearby Petalcingo (Shklovsky 2005) reports stress as 'obscure'.

new_statements.quote: Los valores están integrados como préstamos del español al tseltal en el que la forma original es liméta, tomando en cuenta que el tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo y recae sobre la última silaba de las palabras (véase Polian, 2013: 85), en SS se registran dos valores liméte y liméta, en el que la acentuación se hace en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra al igual que en español, es decir, se mantiene la forma original de la acentuación. SJ presenta también las dos formas, pero además tiene la forma limeté, donde la acentuación cae en la última sílaba de la palabra.
new_statements.translation: The values are integrated as loans from Spanish into Tseltal, in which the original form is liméta; taking into account that Tseltal is a fixed-accent language and the accent falls on the last syllable of words (see Polian 2013: 85), in SS [San Sebastián Bachajón] two values are recorded, liméte and liméta, in which accentuation is on the penultimate syllable of the word as in Spanish, i.e. the original accentuation is kept. SJ [San Jerónimo Bachajón] also has both forms, but in addition has the form limeté, where the accent falls on the last syllable of the word.

The passage is there verbatim: 'Los valores están integrados como préstamos del español al tseltal en el que la forma original es liméta,20 tomando en cuenta que el tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo y recae sobre la última silaba de las palabras (véase Polian, 2013: 85), en SS se registran dos valores liméte y liméta, en el que la acentuación se hace en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra al igual que en español, es decir, se mantiene la forma original de la acentuación. SJ presenta también las dos formas, pero además…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement (Polian 2013 §3.2: fixed final accent) and cites it directly; refines it with Bachajón-specific loanword data showing penult stress retained in Spanish loans in part of the territory, and localises the rule to Bachajón proper (SS vs SJ ejidos). It does not repeat Polian's caveat that the final accent is phrase-level rather than properly a word property.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tseltal (here the Bachajón variety, ejidos San Sebastián and San Jerónimo) has fixed accent on the last syllable of the word; the author cites Polian 2013: 85 for the rule and uses it to explain the adaptation of the Spanish loan limeta. Footnote 20 (p. 83): the original accent pattern liméta is kept in some localities (four in SS, two in SJ) and 'esta palabra está sufriendo una adaptación fonológica al tseltal de BA' (the word is undergoing phonological adaptation to Bachajón Tseltal). Quote as in source (footnote marker '20' after liméta omitted; 'silaba' unaccented in the original).
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loans may keep penultimate stress (liméta, liméte) in some Bachajón localities; the finally-stressed adaptation limeté is recorded in five of seven San Jerónimo localities (PN, JH, RA, KL, XT'), none in San Sebastián.
new_statements.identity_note: tzel1255 is a Glottolog bookkeeping code (ISO tzb Bachajón Tzeltal, merged into tzh). Silvano Jiménez 2014 is specifically about Bachajón (ejidos San Sebastián and San Jerónimo, seven localities in the municipio of Chilón) and so is the closest match to this code; Polian's Guaquitepec materials describe a neighbouring northern-zone town in the same municipio. The existing statement (Polian 2013) is about Oxchuc Tseltal with a footnote on Bachajón.

El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado. [...] El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas, que se pueden caracterizar aproximativamente como los constituyentes prosódicos que agrupan un núcleo léxico y todos sus satélites, incluyendo determinantes, clíticos, preposiciones, etcétera [...] [fn. 2, p. 87:] La prominencia relativa del acento léxico inicial no es la misma en todas las variantes del tseltal. sources.locator: §3.2 'Acento y prosodia', pp. 85-86 (main text) and p. 87 fn. 2 (Bachajón); exceptions p. 85-86 fn. 1 and §3.8.10 'Transfonologización del acento tónico', p. 123. In the saved txt: lines 3364-3466 and 5123-5136.
sources.note: Tseltal is a fixed-accent language with no lexically contrastive accent; the accent falls on the last syllable of the phonological phrase (word + clitics/satellites), realized by F0 rise and lengthening, not intensity; non-final phrases need not be accented; lexical roots may also get an emphatic initial-syllable lengthening, and fn. 2 p. 87 says this initial lexical accent is more important in the Bachajón variety than in Oxchuc. Exceptions: old Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans with initial accent (áko, páta, tsíma), Spanish vowel-final loans keeping penult (káxa, xíla ~ kaxá, xilá).

sources.note: 'Stress is one of the phenomena in Petalcingo Tzeltal that is still quite obscure to me. While Haviland (p.c.) suggests that stress in Mayan languages like Tzotzil and Tzeltal falls on the root, Kaufman 1971 and p.c. argues that word-stress in Tzeltal is word-initial. In my experience, clause-level (prosodic stress) in Petalcingo Tzeltal serves to at least partially obscure word-level stress.'

sources.note: 'stress always falls on the last syllable of a word.. If a root takes a suffix or if it follows a particle, the accent falls on the latter.. Many loan-words retain penultimate stress in the Spanish style (e.g., lóbleh, "oak"), but the older loans have undergone a shift of stress to the final'. Dialect basis (p. 2): a mix of dialects, grammar 'more or less' Oxchuc, but 'We will therefore use the phonetic forms that are found in Mariana Slocum's Bachajón Tzeltal Dictionary'. Pedagogical, not a primary description.

sources.note: §1.4: stress groups (usually = pause groups) of two or more syllables with unifying stress on the final syllable and secondary stress on the first or second syllable; Spanish penult loans normally do not shift. sources.note: Morphophonemic rule (24) p. 31: 'The final syllable of a form has phonemic primary stress when the form precedes a contour (//. ? !//), unless a vowel not more than two syllables earlier has //V́// and no juncture intervenes'; three phonemic stresses (acute, grave, circumflex) §33.3; stressed vowels long in open syllables (§26.5). Southern dialect, not Bachajón.
